business.title: Lithium-ion battery SOH estimation based on degradation physics constraints and cross-attention Transformer-GRU
business.desc: Accurate estimation of lithium-ion battery state of health (SOH) is essential for battery management systems in safety warning, lifetime management, and energy scheduling. To address the difficulty of simultaneously capturing global feature coupling and local degradation memory with a single deep learning model, as well as the lack of degradation-physics constraints in purely data-driven prediction, this paper proposes an SOH estimation method that integrates degradation physics constraints with cross-attention Transformer-GRU, denoted as PI-CTG. First, five health features are extracted from the constant-current/constant-voltage charging-voltage curve and the incremental-capacity (IC) curve, including constant-current charging time, constant-current average voltage, IC peak value, IC peak voltage, and IC average value. Subsequently, the Transformer branch is used to learn the global coupling relationships among health features, the GRU branch is used to capture local degradation memory along the cycle dimension, and the cross-attention module is used to adaptively fuse the two types of representations. Furthermore, the SOH degradation rate is expressed as an implicit function of cycle index and health features, and degradation-dynamics residual and weak monotonicity constraints are incorporated into the training objective. Results on three datasets, namely Oxford, CALCE, and NASA, show that PI-CTG achieves an average RMSE of 0.0072 and an average $$R^2$$ of 0.9730 over six batteries, outperforming the comparison models GRU, Transformer, and CTG without physics constraints. Battery-wise SHAP analysis further shows that constant-current charging time, IC average value, and IC peak value are the major contributing features for SOH estimation, while highly correlated features may exhibit different marginal contributions because of redundancy caused by collinearity.

technology.title: Nuclear localization of the glutaminyl-tRNA synthetase QARS reveals its role in DNA damage response in ovarian cancer
technology.desc: Uncovering novel mechanisms controlling DNA damage response (DDR) is essential to better understand the molecular features of high-grade serous ovarian cancers (HGSOC), which remain a clinical challenge. Here, we demonstrate that the glutaminyl-tRNA-synthetase QARS is a key player in DDR. We show that QARS is regulated at translational level by the MAPK pathway in HGSOC and controls homologous recombination (HR) through a translation-independent mechanism. Analyses combining RNA sequencing, immunohistochemistry, proteomic data and functional assays from HGSOC patient cohorts and relevant cellular models reveal that QARS promotes DNA repair via the HR pathway. Interestingly, we uncover that QARS is located in the nucleus and is enriched at chromatin upon DNA damage. Nuclear QARS controls HR by interacting with the nuclear autoantigen SP100, a major component of PML-nuclear bodies (PML-NB), that are regulatory hubs for DNA repair proteins. Our data highlight nuclear functions and mechanisms for QARS involving SP100, PML-NB and MRE11 that enhance HR in HGSOC. Here, the authors find that the glutaminyl-tRNA synthetase QARS, a cytosolic protein involved in mRNA translation, relocates to the nucleus to promote homologous recombination (HR). QARS promotes HR by interacting with SP100 to maintain PML-NB integrity and MRN complex localization, thus reducing tumor sensitivity to treatment.

world.title: SIGNIS: SIGNIS President Urges Congress Delegates to Turn AI Discussions into Concrete Action for Evangelisation
world.desc:
Sarah Pelaji
The President of SIGNIS World, Ms. Helen Osman, urged Catholic media professionals to ensure that discussions on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital communication result in concrete actions that advance the Church's mission of evangelisation and promote the well-being of humanity.
She said this during a video call on 4th August 2026, at the Opening of the Seventh SIGNIS World Congress, held in Kigali, Rwanda, under the theme Digital Communication for Communion, Equity and Environmental Well-being.
The SIGNIS World Congress brought together Catholic communicators from around the world to reflect on how digital technologies can be used responsibly to foster human dignity, solidarity, and the Church's evangelising mission.
She gave the message after reading a goodwill message sent from Rome by a former President of SIGNIS World, who could not attend the Congress.
She welcomed the theme of the Congress, pointing out that it is closely linked with Pope Leo XIV's most recent Encyclical Letter, Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in an era of AI.
She hoped that the Congress would result in not only plans but concrete decisions which would help to further the Church's evangelising mission and at the same time contribute to the spiritual and material well-being of people all over the world.
She appreciated the leadership of SIGNIS World in bringing the international Congress to Africa and acknowledged   Fr. Prof. Walter Chikwendu Ihejirika, President of SIGNIS Africa and Chairperson of the Africa Organising Committee, for his leadership in organising the global gathering.
She expressed confidence in the success of the Congress and mentioned Africa's historic role in Catholic communications, since it had hosted the 1983 World Congresses of the former UNDA (International Catholic Association for Radio and Television) and OCIC (International Catholic Organisation for Cinema and Audiovisuals) in Nairobi, Kenya, organisations which later merged to form SIGNIS.
The goodwill message ended by offering prayerful best wishes for a successful Congress and for God's blessings upon SIGNIS World as it goes on with its promotion of ethical, faith-based communication in the service of the Gospel and the common good.
